newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK to raise interest rates gradually-poll.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK to raise interest rates gradually-poll.

text.p: The next British government is unlikely to raise interest rates drastically in the year after the election, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

While most agree that interest rates are on their way up, they said the climb would be more of a stroll than a hike, with the base rate up only 100 basis points from its current 5.75 percent level by the end of the second quarter of 1998.

"Because of spare capacity and slower growth earlier in the cycle, the rise in interest rates necessary to keep down inflation will not be particularly sharp by historical standards," said Trevor Williams, economic adviser at Lloyds TSB Group.
He put base rates at 6.25 percent in second-quarter 1998.
The poll, which was carried out between September 30 and October 2, showed economists expect base rates to rise by 25 basis points by the end of the second quarter next year.
A general election must be held by May 1997 and opinion polls give the opposition Labour party a substantial lead over the ruling Conservatives.
Whoever comes to power, economists said some monetary tightening would be necessary to dampen inflation and push economic growth back to trend levels.

"We're going to see particularly strong growth during 1997, considerably in excess of Britain's productive potential, because of strong consumption and investment activity," said Steve Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International.
"That means we will need to see some tightening of monetary policy in order to contain inflation".
The poll predicted base rates rising to 6.75 percent in the second quarter of 1998, with forecasts ranging from around 5.50 percent to 7.75 percent.
Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has cut rates four times since December, overriding the objections of the Bank of England on the last occasion in June.

Central bank governor Eddie George, worried about future inflationary pressures, argued at the July monetary meeting that official rates should now be at 6.0 percent, but Clarke over-ruled his advice.
Some economists believe Clarke has been motivated by political considerations rather than sound economics, a charge he robustly denies.
"Clarke could have kept policy tighter -- it would have helped to keep inflation down," Williams said. "The pressure was on him politically to keep interest rates low to keep the economy going."
Economists say the rate cuts may mean the Chancellor fails to meet his own inflation target.
In July the chancellor pledged to get RPIX (retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments) down to 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 2.25 percent by the following year.
The Reuters poll predicted core inflation at 2.6 percent and 3.0 percent over the same periods, with monetary easing, increased retail margins and burgeoning producer prices fueling price pressures.
"Manufacturing prices will pick up fairly sharply as the sector picks up but retail margins will be the driver," said Hannah.
High street sales soared in August, displaying further evidence of a rebound in the consumer sector, but the figures effectively slammed the door on more interest rate cuts, economists said.
Even though rate increases may not be steep by historical standards, a small rise combined with a tougher fiscal stance would be sufficient to bring growth back to manageable levels, economists said.

The poll predicted GDP would grow by 3.5 percent in the second quarter of next year, around the time of an election, but as monetary policy tightened, growth would ease off, dipping to 2.7 percent in the second quarter of 1998.
"Growth will slow as the incoming government starts tightening both fiscal and monetary policy," said James McKay, UK economist at Paine Webber.

"Putting things into perspective, we're likely to see pretty strong growth rates well above trend...Some kind of policy action will have to be taken to bring growth back into line and make it non-inflationary."
